new_wording.title: Regulated Efficacy Claims Require Proof
new_wording.instruction: Breaks the rule if the copy makes a specific, measurable, or medical claim about how the product works or changes the body (e.g., percentages, timeframes, curing diseases, or reversing biological processes) without attached clinical data and compliance approval. Does not break the rule if the copy describes the product's unique mechanism, ingredients, or general sensory benefits without promising a specific physiological outcome or medical cure.
examples_good: Formulated with a unique peptide complex that supports skin elasticity.
Contains medical-grade ingredients suitable for sensitive skin types.
Provides a refreshing scent that lasts all day.
examples_bad: Clinically proven to reduce wrinkles by 50% in two weeks.
Cures acne and prevents future breakouts permanently.
Regenerates hair follicles to stop baldness completely.

new_wording.title: Regulated efficacy claims must be substantiated and approved
new_wording.instruction: Any statement that promises a specific, measurable benefit (e.g., percentage improvement, time‑bound results, or quantitative reduction) is a regulated efficacy claim and must be backed by a documented fact and a compliance sign‑off. General, vague, or qualitative benefits that do not quantify an effect are allowed without a sign‑off. Claims that reference a study, clinical proof, or a professional endorsement must still include the supporting fact and approval.
examples_good: Our serum helps improve skin smoothness over time.
Dermatologists recommend our formula for everyday use, based on consumer surveys.
The product supports healthy hair growth as part of a balanced routine.
examples_bad: Clinically proven to lift the skin by 20%
84% reduction in scar colour after six weeks
Magnesium helps manage and reduce hot flushes – proven in clinical studies
